issues.legal_issue: A petition invoking the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction is distinct from a writ petition, and procedural rules cannot convert one into the other.
material_facts: The petition expressly invoked the High Court’s writ jurisdiction, stated that no efficacious remedy was available, and sought certiorari to quash the lower appellate court’s decision.
The petition was filed and described as a writ petition; the argument that it should instead be treated as a supervisory petition was rejected.
The applicable High Court rules dealt separately with writ petitions and applications invoking supervisory jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The petition was a writ petition, not a petition under the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction; a petition invoking supervisory jurisdiction cannot be called a writ petition.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution confer distinct powers: Article 226 provides original writ jurisdiction, whereas Article 227 confers supervisory jurisdiction and does not authorize issuance of a writ. A petition under Article 227 is not a writ petition, and High Court rules cannot alter that constitutional distinction. The Court relied on the separate treatment of the two proceedings in the Bombay High Court (Appellate Side) Rules and on Jhaman Karamsingh Dadlani v. Ramanlal Maneklal Kantawala, AIR 1975 Bombay 182.

predicates.petition_expressly_invokes_writ_remedy: The applicant expressly presents the proceeding as a request for the High Court to exercise its writ jurisdiction.
predicates.petition_seeks_quashing_by_certiorari: The applicant asks the High Court to quash an inferior court’s decision by certiorari.

issues.definition: When an applicant expressly seeks writ relief and asks for certiorari, the proceeding is a writ proceeding rather than a supervisory petition.

issues.legal_issue: A writ petition is not an appropriate remedy for a private property dispute between private parties when no public or statutory duty, statutory infraction, or collusion with the State is involved.
material_facts: The underlying case was a landlord-tenant dispute concerning possession of premises and alleged damage to property.
The dispute was between private parties, and the landlord was the only respondent to the High Court petition.
The respondent was not shown to be performing a public or statutory duty, acting in collusion with the State, or involved in an infraction of statute.
The petition expressly invoked writ jurisdiction and sought to set aside the lower appellate court’s decision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in entertaining the writ petition in this private landlord-tenant dispute. Its refusal to interfere with the concurrent factual findings was nevertheless unexceptionable, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 provides a public-law remedy, not a forum to decide private property rights. Ordinarily a writ cannot issue against a private person unless that person performs a public or statutory duty; a private person may be amenable where there is collusion with the State. The Court relied on Sohan Lal v. Union of India, AIR 1957 SC 529; Engineering Mazdoor Sabha v. Hind Cycles Ltd., AIR 1963 SC 874; Rohtas Industries Ltd. v. Rohtas Industries Staff Union, (1976) 2 SCC 82; Mohammed Hanif v. State of Assam, (1969) 2 SCC 782; T.C. Basappa v. T. Nagappa, AIR 1954 SC 440; Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. Kalyani Banerjee, (1973) 1 SCC 273; State of Rajasthan v. Bhawani Singh, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 306; Mohan Pandey v. Usha Rani Rajgaria, (1992) 4 SCC 61; Prasanna Kumar Roy Karmakar v. State of W.B., (1996) 3 SCC 403; and P.R. Murlidharan v. Swami Dharmananda Theertha Padar, (2006) 4 SCC 501.

rule.if: article_226_writ_petition and private_property_dispute and private_respondent and not respondent_performs_public_or_statutory_duty and not state_collusion and not statutory_infraction

predicates.article_226_writ_petition: The applicant seeks relief through the High Court’s original writ jurisdiction.
predicates.private_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns property rights disputed between private individuals.
predicates.private_respondent: The person against whom relief is sought is a private individual.
predicates.respondent_performs_public_or_statutory_: The respondent performs a public or statutory duty relevant to the requested relief.
predicates.state_collusion: The private respondent acts in collusion with the State in the conduct challenged.
predicates.statutory_infraction: The challenged conduct involves an infraction of statute.

issues.definition: A writ petition is not maintainable when it concerns private property rights against a private respondent who performs no relevant public or statutory duty, with neither State collusion nor a statutory infraction.

issues.legal_issue: The High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction over subordinate courts is exceptional and cannot be used as an appellate power to correct ordinary errors of fact or law.
material_facts: The challenge concerned decisions of subordinate civil courts in a private landlord-tenant proceeding.
The lower courts had made concurrent findings of fact, and the High Court declined to interfere with them.
The Supreme Court stated that supervisory intervention is confined to keeping subordinate courts within the bounds of their authority and to exceptional failures of justice.
issues.conclusion: Supervisory interference is warranted only in exceptional circumstances, including jurisdictional excess or refusal, a patent perversion, gross or manifest failure of justice, or violation of basic principles of natural justice; it is not available merely to correct an ordinary factual or legal error or to substitute another possible view.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 confers discretionary supervisory jurisdiction, not appellate jurisdiction. The High Court may intervene to keep subordinate courts within the bounds of their authority, including where they assume jurisdiction they lack, fail to exercise jurisdiction they possess, or exercise jurisdiction in a manner not permitted by law resulting in failure of justice. The Court relied on Waryam Singh v. Amarnath, AIR 1954 SC 215; Dalmia Jain Airways Ltd. v. Sukumar Mukherjee, AIR 1951 Calcutta 193; Manmatha Nath Biswas v. Emperor, AIR 1933 Calcutta 132; Nagendra Nath Bora v. Commissioner of Hills Division and Appeals, AIR 1958 SC 398; State of Gujarat v. Vakhatsinghji Vajesinghji Vaghela, AIR 1968 SC 1481; Mani Nariman Daruwala v. Phiroz N. Bhatena, (1991) 3 SCC 141; Chandavarkar Sita Ratna Rao v. Ashalata S. Guram, (1986) 4 SCC 447; Laxmikant Revchand Bhojwani v. Pratapsingh Mohansingh Pardeshi, (1995) 6 SCC 576; and Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai, (2003) 6 SCC 675. The Court also held that curtailment of the revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not expand supervisory jurisdiction, and cited L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, (1997) 3 SCC 261, on Article 227’s constitutional status.

rule.if: supervisory_challenge_to_subordinate_court and (jurisdictional_overreach or jurisdictional_refusal or unlawful_jurisdictional_exercise_causing_injustice or patent_perversity or gross_failure_of_justice or basic_natural_justice_breach)

predicates.supervisory_challenge_to_subordinate_cou: A party challenges a subordinate court’s decision by seeking supervisory review.
predicates.jurisdictional_overreach: The subordinate court assumes authority it does not possess.
predicates.jurisdictional_refusal: The subordinate court refuses to exercise authority it possesses.
predicates.unlawful_jurisdictional_exercise_causing: The subordinate court exercises its authority in a manner not permitted by law and that causes failure of justice or grave injustice.
predicates.patent_perversity: The subordinate court’s decision is patently perverse.
predicates.gross_failure_of_justice: The subordinate court’s decision results in a gross or manifest failure of justice.
predicates.basic_natural_justice_breach: The subordinate court’s process violates basic principles of natural justice.

issues.definition: Supervisory interference is permissible in a challenge to a subordinate court only when at least one exceptional jurisdictional or justice-related defect is present.
